1 oz Domaine du Manoir de Montreuil Calvados (Morin Selection)
1 oz Navarre Pineau des Charentes (Guerin)
1/2 oz Rhum JM VSOP (Clement)
3/4 oz Lemon Juice
1/2 oz Simple Syrup

Shake with ice and strain into a coupe glass.
Two Mondays ago, I sought out more uses for my new bottle of Pineau des Charentes, so I looked to the Death & Co.: Welcome Home book and found the Rockabilly. The drink was created by Adam Griggs in 2019 as a riff on the classic Pompadour – a recipe from Frank Meier's 1934 The Artistry Of Mixing Drinks which pairs the fortified wine with an aged rhum agricole and lemon juice. I made the Pompadour back in 2011 when I last purchased a bottle of Pineau des Charentes, and here, the concept was taken in an apple direction. Once mixed, the Rockabilly gave forth an apple, floral, and nectarine aroma. Next, lemon notes on the sip danced their way into apple, funky rum, melon, and fresh apricot flavors on the swallow.

content:
Last Friday, Reddit had its worst day since its IPO, with a drop of almost 30%1. It didn’t matter that they beat their third-quarter estimates; what mattered most was a weak Q4 forecast and the quote from Reddit CEO Steve Huffman, “Our search referral traffic was down meaningfully in Q3, with the decline accelerating later in the quarter.” He also wrote, “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week.”

There’s no baseline to understand whether 1 million referrals is a lot or a little, but there is no doubt a stock dropping 30% in a day is a lot.

Reddit, which I am certain looks at the data daily, has seen this coming for years; hence their other announcements that shape a larger strategy:

  • Testing a logged-in-only experience outside the U.S.
  • Shutting down RSS feeds
  • Shutting down the public API
  • Moving data access to its Developer Platform, which makes all Reddit data access paid only.

The Three Dots Are Pretty Easy to Connect

Dot #1: Traditional Google search: you search for X, Google searches for X and provides a list of high-quality X links, which — if the links are high quality — means you click on X, which is a Reddit post about X.

Google would greatly prefer if you didn’t click on X because the moment you do, you’ve left Google and they’ve mostly lost their ability to present you with advertising. You read that right: the reason you go to Google is to find other high-quality stuff that they don’t want you to actually see. My favorite attempt was AMP, Accelerated Mobile Pages, where publishers built lightweight copies of their content, and Google served them from their own servers. Yes, you were promised a traffic advantage, but you lose control over design, ads, and analytics.

Google dropped AMP’s search perks in 2021 in the face of continued criticism, but all they really had to do was wait a few years because a vastly better solution would present itself.

Dot #2: I’m guessing sometime in 2022, all the AI players started sucking down all the data in order to train ever-improving models. The more data? The better the models. It’s vastly more complicated than that, but alarms at Reddit apparently started going off in April of 2023, when they moved to charge for API access. The CEO quote: “… [w]e don’t need to give all of that value to some of the largest companies in the world for free.”

While content producers perhaps saw a massive theft of intellectual property, content consumers did not. What they eventually saw was the eerily accurate answer to the dumb throwaway question they typed into their first chatbot. They thought, “Golly, that’s cool.”2 Sub-dot thought: Like Google, AI players have paradoxical motivations: the goal is to get you to use the services so they can help, but helping doesn’t pay the bills. Using more tokens is the business, which means that, like Google, the gig is to keep helping whether you want the help or not.

Dot #3: Present day. Google has a feature called AI Overviews, which you’ve already seen. It’s a human-sounding summary that attempts to answer your questions. There is no way to turn it off — it exists to keep you on Google. The research shows that when an AI Overview shows, clicks on the first result drop 58%. More than half the folks who would have clicked that top result are no longer leaving, which means more sweet, sweet ad revenue.

That’s Not the Dot

I’ve spent the past decade watching the blogging community vanish. There are the stalwarts, but the vast majority of bloggers either stopped or left for lighter-weight walled gardens. Sure, blogging was a fad. Writing, however, is not. I get it — it’s easier to write a pithy one-line Reddit post than a fully fleshed-out thought. Guilty as charged.

I giggle when folks mention Google is in trouble because of declining search usage. First, decades of search habits will take time to disassemble and reassemble. Second, if you are using Google Search less, I’m guessing you’re still using Gmail and similar Google services. If you’re like me and have wired the robots into Gmail, you’re using Gmail significantly more. Yes, I’ve turned off every switch that says “don’t train on me,” but go throw those switches yourself and report on how confident you are that you flipped them all successfully.

I started this piece with Reddit because the company provides a service that creates tremendous value, and I’m not talking about the monetary value; I’m talking about the social value. Early on in my robot journeys, I asked Claude to source any fact it shared with me. I skimmed the sources and was surprised to see how often a random Reddit post was the source of the robot’s thoughts.

Yes, the robot sucked down all the books (including all of mine). Yes, they did the same with countless images, as well. I feel we haven’t yet seen the full set of legal consequences, but that’s not the dot: it’s the value of humans talking with other humans, building things for each other — often simple, frequently hilarious, and doing the work to document why they did what they did… because they want to help.

This was supposed to be a brief introduction to a new feature I’m launching on Rands on Tuesday, but it turned into a whole bunch of dots explaining the disproportionate value of what happens when humans hang with other humans.

See you Tuesday.

  1. This drop was certainly amplified by a broad AI bubble sell-off that isn’t close to over.
  2. No one except me thought those exact words.

content:
Powerful AI is unpredictable. Your robotic butler may suddenly decide to kill you1 for no comprehensible reason, in the same way that Bing’s helpful chat AI would sometimes try to blackmail or seduce its users. “Solving alignment” means understanding even superintelligent AI minds well enough to be confident they’ll never do that. As I see it, solving alignment for LLMs isn’t just impossible, it’s incoherent: we can’t even articulate what it would look like to succeed.

LLMs are not blind optimizers

Prior to LLMs, AI safety researchers thought AI would be a “blind optimizer”: like a chess engine, it would be superhumanly focused on achieving some fixed goal. If the goal wasn’t safe (for instance, “manufacture cheap paperclips”), a powerful AI might wreak havoc on the way to achieving it. Aligning AI thus meant figuring out how to specify the right goal. This is harder than it sounds2, but it’s at least possible to imagine it happening.

Unfortunately, modern LLMs aren’t like chess engines. Instead of being trained on some concrete verifiable reward3, they’re trained to imitate a giant, highly-varied corpus of human writing. This makes them weird. They contain a nearly infinite array of personalities, which they seamlessly switch between based on their inputs. Frontier AI labs try hard to make these personalities safe and stable, but there are still many strange cases where LLMs seem to switch into mysterious or dangerous personas.

The problem here is that LLMs don’t have fixed goals. There’s nothing that you could, even in principle, formally specify in order to constrain their behavior. The “goals” that LLMs do have are informal, organic, multifarious, and constantly shifting as the dominant persona (or blend of personas) changes. They’re nicknamed shoggoths for a reason. So we can’t align them by specifying their goal. Instead, we have to try the other approach: understanding them well enough that we can be sure they’re safe. And unfortunately that approach is doomed from the start.

It is impossible in principle to understand LLMs

What does it mean to ask for a full understanding — or full enough understanding — of why an LLM generates some token? In one sense, we have that already, because we can mechanistically trace through the calculations involved. But we don’t know what those calculations mean. Saying that Grok called itself “MechaHitler” because these billion weights multiplied in this way doesn’t tell us why Grok did it. What we would need for alignment purposes is a more human-like and less mechanical sense of understanding: a full understanding of motive.

To see why a full understanding of motive is a foolish thing to ask for, imagine asking it about a human. Suppose you were hiring a nanny or electing a president and you wanted to be sure that they were going to act in your interests4. Humans sometimes do very surprising things out of nowhere, after all. Would it be sensible to ask for a full understanding of that person’s mind, in order to reassure yourself that they would act in the way you wanted? Of course not.

It’s meaningless to even talk about a “full understanding” in this sense, because the mind is not a mechanism that operates via clean, understandable abstractions. It is a morass of electric and chemical impulses from which a “self” bubbles up5. There are no motives of the kind you’re looking for! Motives bottom out early on, and tracing the causal chain beyond that can only be done mechanistically: i.e. unhelpfully, for the same reason that explanations based on model weights are unhelpful.

Why mechanistic interpretability is doomed

Couldn’t a sufficiently detailed mechanistic explanation give us the confidence we need? The best we’ve got along those lines right now are the tools of “mechanistic interpretability”: features, neurons, probes, and circuits. You observe the model doing something, see which parts of its “brain” light up6, and correlate those with some pattern of behavior. If you can then induce that pattern by artificially boosting that part of the “brain”, you can claim victory. Even assuming total success, this program cannot deliver us the kind of understanding we’re looking for.

First, we label patterns based on behavior we observe, but the main misalignment case we’re worried about — the LLM suddenly performing some shocking harmful action — is definitionally something we aren’t going to observe before it happens. We can’t identify a feature without first eliciting its behavior7, and we can only elicit a small subset of potential model bad behavior. There will always be many untracked failure modes.

Second, the labels we apply to patterns are our guesses, and may be wrong. The philosopher Kripke famously argued that, until you run into the relevant case, there’s no meaningful difference between the “addition” rule and the “quaddition” rule (a version of addition where if either number is greater than 57 the answer is always 5). Likewise, the LLM feature we call “kindness” might be “kindness unless the year is 2030”, or “kindness unless the LLM is in a position to cause mass casualties”, and so on. Those features are completely indistinguishable8 from our perspective.

Third, even an exhaustive well-labeled map of features and patterns would not give us certainty that a model could not go rogue. The full combination of features involved in any model action would be far, far too complex to interpret. For instance, if a model has “evil” lit up, is it because it’s trying to avoid evil, or trying to cause it, or trying to combat it, or is worried about some hypothetical evil action, or is anticipating that a user might make the judgement? We would have many, many billions of questions like that to answer per-token. Far too many for a human to comprehend9, certainly.

Could some hypothetical, radically different kind of mechanistic interpretability somehow predict all possible actions a model might take in advance and rule out actions like “kill all humans”? I think this at least could be semantically coherent, but it runs into the problem above. Models can accept a near-infinite array of inputs and give a near-infinite array of outputs. This definitely cannot be comprehended by a human, only by another model, which itself would have to be checked by another model, and so on.

Conclusion

If you think solving LLM alignment is possible, I would love to read your description of what it would even look like for us to understand LLMs well enough to be sure they’re safe. I would love to know if you think humans are similarly understandable in principle (and if not, what makes LLMs different). It seems to me that if we think clearly about the topic, we don’t even know what it would mean to be confident that we have aligned an LLM properly10, because “motive” simply doesn’t exist at the level of detail we’d need.

Of course, we have mitigations in place. Chain-of-thought monitoring is surprisingly helpful for a mechanism that appeared by accident, so long as we never train on reasoning tokens themselves. We can sandbox models and put humans-in-the-loop and watch for feature activations and so on. But it’s been well understood since the early 2000s that these are insufficient11 to detect or control a superintelligence. Whether you think mitigations are enough depends on whether you take superintelligence seriously.

Mechanistic interpretability is still a useful field. Extracting features can help us train models that do less reward-hacking and are more helpful under ordinary circumstances. There’s just no way it will ever solve the problem of LLM agents going rogue and causing massive harm, because the kind of understanding we’d need to prevent that is impossible in principle.

  1. It’s relevant to note that humans sometimes do this too. From Vaneigem: “One fine morning, the faithful lackey, who has hitherto identified completely with his master, leaps on his oppressor and slits his throat.”

    ↩

  2. For instance, the goal “eliminate suffering” is best satisfied by destroying all humans, the goal “maximise everyone’s happiness” is best satisfied by hooking everyone up to a fentanyl IV, and so on. It’s also very difficult to find a way to translate concepts like “happiness” and “well-being” into a formal goal, and if you get it wrong, the difference between the concept and your formalization is likely to lead to dire consequences.

    ↩

  3. Yes, I know LLMs are partially trained in this way, but being RLVRed on millions of different rewards does not produce a coherent goal. There’s no way to formalize in advance the utility function that RLVR instils in the model, and no way even to reliably predict how it will interact with the goals and personas that emerge from the base model.

    ↩

  4. Of course, for humans you can rely on institutions, social proof, and so on. This doesn’t work for superintelligent LLMs because they (a) arrive fully-formed with no social proof and (b) are smart enough to be much more dangerous than a single rogue human. (Incidentally, the LLMs I asked to review this post were obsessed with this point, and wanted me to elevate it into the main thrust of the post).

    ↩

  5. Perhaps as an epiphenomenon. If you’re interested in this idea and want to see it taken further, I recommend (but do not endorse the ideas in) Blindsight.

    ↩

  6. Which parts of the model’s internal state have high values, for instance.

    ↩

  7. That doesn’t mean we have to deliberately elicit one feature at a time — dictionary learning works by just running arbitrary content through the model and seeing what lights up — but it does mean that we have to actually trigger the behavior in order to see it.

    ↩

  8. If you’re thinking “well, but isn’t the simple feature more likely via Occam’s Razor”, I recommend browsing through NeuronPersonas (the linked feature is “Nervous Person Waiting To Be Let Go Who Escalates Ammonia Solution Concentrations”).

    ↩

  9. I’ve heard people punt on this question by saying “well, of course I couldn’t use a fully-mapped LLM brain to figure out if it’s dangerous, but another smart model could”. This is not a satisfying answer because you’d have to also ensure that your warden model was behaving (with a third model, perhaps?)

    ↩

  10. Of course we can articulate what alignment looks like: the model never does anything bad. We just can’t articulate what it would look like to know the model was aligned.

    ↩

  11. For more on that, see my post on superpersuasion: the model will simply outwit or bribe any human in the loop. For a credible source who understands modern mechanistic interpretability, see Neel Nanda, who I read as broadly agreeing with me.

    ↩

content:
If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.

Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it.

That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone.

Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself.

Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear.

This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions.

Table of Contents

  1. Scott Alexander’s Core Claims.
  2. My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims.
  3. Briefly on Alignment.
  4. Probabilities and How They Work.
  5. Building a Thing That Might Kill Everyone is Deontologically Evil.
  6. People Quitting Major Labs While Raising Alarms Obviously Works.
  7. On AI Forecasting.
  8. Advancing Capabilities Burns Timeline.
  9. But China.
  10. Ethical People Can Disagree With You.
  11. There Are More Than Two Outcomes.
  12. Efforts Are Complementary, Not Mutually Exclusive.
  13. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
  14. Vaniver is Not Convinced.
  15. There Is No Consensus That We Should Exclusively Focus on Plan A.
  16. It’s Not the Incentives, It’s You.
  17. Anthropic Is Not Optimally Pursuing These Plans.
  18. Against Against Sura.

Scott Alexander’s Core Claims

Scott Alexander writes Against SURA, or the strategy of calling upon nations and companies building superintelligence to stop building it and calling upon employees of those labs to quit, even without reciprocity.

Here is his definition and coinage:

I’ll lump these ideas together under the heading of “SURA” – the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA’s platform as:

  • Individual alignment-pilled AI companies are morally obligated to stop unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect race dynamics to continue in their absence.
  • Individual alignment-pilled employees at these companies should quit, regardless of whether they’re in capabilities or alignment roles, and regardless of whether they think their company is morally better than its competitors.
  • Individual alignment-pilled countries (for example, a hypothetical future alignment-pilled US) should ban or heavily restrict AI progress unilaterally, regardless of whether they expect other countries (for example, China) to continue racing in their absence.

I mostly avoid quoting directly from the OP, since most of you likely read it.

Scott’s basic frame of the situation is that there are two classes of plan:

  1. Plan A, his combination of AI 2040’s Plans A/S/Other, are plans that involve working for a global pause in AI development.
  2. Plan C, his combination of everything else, is where we don’t do that.

Scott’s core arguments are that (this is my ITT summary of Scott):

  1. Many actions that aim to help your chances of pulling off Plan A hurt your chances of survival if Plan A fails and you are forced back into Plan C.
    1. Plan C benefits from ‘alignment-pilling’ the companies, whereas Plan A benefits from raising mass awareness, educating politicians and getting verification tech.
    2. SURA is one of the actions that hurts Plan C.
  2. Plan A is first best, and we should try to do it, but it probably won’t happen, and a large portion of our victories come from executing Plan C.
  3. The correct and traditional strategy is to support Plan A while also preparing to execute Plan C as best we can.
  4. SURA, telling whoever listens to unilaterally stop, de facto torches our chances for execution of Plan C in order to maximize the chances of getting to try Plan A.
  5. SURA is an increasingly popular strategy, but it only makes sense if you believe some combination of assumptions.
    1. Alignment is highly doomed, or is highly doomed under Plan C conditions.
    2. Racing to superintelligence under these conditions is deontologically evil.
    3. Racing burns valuable time.
    4. People quitting is helpful in raising awareness and pursuing a pause.
  6. SURA is actually bad for even your chances of getting Plan A.
  7. There is currently a ‘consensus in favor of SURA’ in rationalist/EA spaces.

Scott also makes other claims, such as his overview of alignment. In many cases the claims seem overgeneralized or overstated.

I respond to Scott’s claims, and without any implicit endorsement of claims I do not mention.

My High Level Responses To Scott’s Core Claims

  1. True in general, but often false for specific actions where it is claimed.
    1. These actions all help both Plan A and Plan C, although they differentially help their respective plans more.
    2. If fully executed, yes. On the margin, the sign of impact is not obvious.
  2. True, given our uncertainty over the situation. I agree with Scott Alexander that this is his strongest point.
    1. There are those who disagree, and I respect the opposite position.
  3. True for the world overall, in aggregate. Not obviously true for an individual or group, and not obviously true on the margin.
  4. Extreme forms of SURA can be negative for Plan C, but on net and on the margin while sign is unclear I expect reasonable ones to be positive even for Plan C.
  5. These are key arguments in favor of SURA, but even if all four were false it would not definitively render SURA a bad idea, as this is not an exhaustive list.
    1. I have high model uncertainty on this. I respect those who think alignment under Plan C is highly doomed. They have good arguments. I am not fully convinced. Alignment under Plan C could turn out to be highly doomed, or building superintelligence could be highly doomed even if alignment is solved, or it is possible that alignment is ‘super doable’ although difficult.
    2. I am not a deontologist, but yeah, it seems rather deontologically evil. You might want to do it anyway, and at some point in a cost-benefit analysis you have to be willing to as Rao says Be Slightly Evil, but don’t pretend otherwise.
      1. Scott’s attempt to draw a parallel to frontier AI use feels very confused here. Obviously we don’t want to go full Asymmetric Justice. I’m pretty appalled by trying to say that actively working to develop the thing that might kill everyone is the same thing as the marginal economic impact of personal use of frontier models. This is just the ‘if I don’t do the evil thing, someone else will, so it’s fine to do it’ argument and I fully reject it.
    3. This seems obviously true to some extent. But we can talk price, both in terms of how much time and how valuable is that time.
    4. This again seems obviously true to me and we should be talking price.
  6. False in expectation on the margin for Plan A, arguably for Plan C as well per #4.
  7. False. There is not a consensus on this question. Even a weak version of this (with some amount of fallback) is a minority position, and the full version is rare.

Briefly on Alignment

It is not Scott’s main point, but I want to flag that I strongly disagree with Scott’s stated model of alignment. I do not believe that AI models are well-modeled as ‘inheriting virtue’ simply because they learn to imitate humans. If nothing else, this implies that AI base models are “virtuous” until you “corrupt” them with RLVR. No. This is at best highly misleading.

This was a plausible candidate for the worst thing in the post.

I do agree with Scott’s general theory of what Plan C alignment success looks like, in that it involves trying to string prosaic stopgaps together long enough to let the AI pivot to doing our alignment homework for us, and hopefully its alignment can become self-reinforcing and antifragile. I agree that this seems potentially possible, but I also think it is very easy to see multiple places where a p(doom) of 90%+ could come from, including:

  1. Even if we do ‘solve alignment’ our current plans on what to do with the resulting AIs would still doom us, and we can’t even properly discuss this in public, so it seems highly likely we will turn the world state unwinnable anyway, and die.
  2. Even if we can ‘solve alignment’ with strong implementation of prosaic alignment strategies leading to automated alignment research, the current quality of play inside the labs says we would very likely fail to execute on this anyway, and die.
  3. We are highly uncertain that the above prosaic strategy is viable even if done well.

The most obvious and common reason for a very high p(doom) is to believe, in the style of Eliezer Yudkowsky, that alignment requires you to hit a very precise target, on the first try, while dodging a rather large List of Lethalities. They argue that asking AIs to automate the alignment research will inevitably mean they miss key elements or otherwise fail. I think that is super reasonable, and it is strange to me that Scott Alexander finds this hard to understand.

Probabilities and How They Work

This exchange has some abridged responses.

Oliver Habryka: But yeah, I think you should obviously be willing to risk war if a foreign lab is working towards building ASI.

Scott Alexander: I think these considerations apply in a small fraction of worlds where the US government is very alignment-pilled but China isn’t.

… Under my model a really good Plan C+ has an 90%+ chance of working.

Oliver Habryka: God man, I really find it extremely wild to think that we will solve the alignment problem with an expected 6-12 month lead, in a unilateral fashion and thereafter declare the end of history.

Certainly if you say, as Scott does, that ‘new members are unaware that Plan C was ever a possibility’ I am deeply, deeply confused.

Similarly, you can define the AI safety community as those people who think solving alignment is doomed or assert this as per Janus, but that seems very wrong given many of them work on solving alignment and many others say it is solvable.

If anything my view is far closer to that of Oliver Habryka here, that the bulk of efforts broadly around Lighthaven and the rationalist and EA communities have been to get power at labs or start new labs, and that this has been the primary counterfactual impact of efforts so far, for both better and worse.

Oliver Habryka: Man, IDK, like 75% of efforts around me have gone into somehow trying to get power at the labs or starting new labs. Even on just a resource competition this has been the primary strategy and people in that strategy have been the primary people who have e.g. told anyone trying to make an x-risk focused think tank in DC to shut up as to not upset their delicate political machinations.

I imagine a world where there was a very public CLTR-like think tank in DC that had been publishing compute regulation playbooks for years, about 3x more people putting their efforts into talking publicly about existential risk from AI, and organizations like METR needing to navigate around vastly fewer conflicts of interest that genuinely jeopardize their ability to do their job.

The dynamics here go a lot deeper and more things would be different, but this is where my visualization would start.

My model of Scott thinks that the existing strategy in DC of lots of people trying to play various inside games is great, and he is supportive of the people who have been trying to get the people who are louder about the concerns to shut up, because he does think that being more open that way will cost lots of social capital.

I think everyone agrees there should be a DC angle, the question is how much does that involve people seeking power and doing various inside-game like things, and to what degree does that involve people speaking openly about the risks and building popular support. These two have historically been very drastically in conflict (and the former coalition has been enormously dominant in DC EA as far as I can tell).

Scott Alexander: Am I unfairly mischaracterizing you, or are you doing the thing I warned about in my post of describing support for SURA as “speaking openly” and support for any non-SURA view as “seeking power”? These two axes seem in-principle orthogonal to me, although maybe correlated in real life just through personalities.

Oliver Habryka: I would certainly not describe the support for *any* non-SURA views as “seeking power”.

I think writing honestly and openly about your worries and fears is not generally “seeking power”, though of course it can then be used for coalition-building, but it’s a different kind of power.

Similarly, I don’t think you are “seeking power” by writing your anti-SURA post.

But you are generally much more in favor of the power-seeking strategies of people in DC than I am. Those people are mostly against SURA, though occasionally in-favor.

I think the correlation here is substantially explained causally, in the sense that if your plan is “me and my coalition just need to get as much lead as possible” then of course you don’t want to wake up the world to what’s happening. You want to avoid both waking up other countries, and avoid waking up other coalitions that might then compete with you for control of the AI-adjacent parts of the government or company you are at.

You broadly seem supportive of this strategy, and indeed I think most “successful” racing strategies rely on going pretty hard on it. You yourself are executing a strategy I like much more, and I wouldn’t have that many issues (though still some) with lots of people doing the exact thing you are doing (where you argue about your position publicly and take the hit on the part of their strategy that relies on being covert). But mostly, that’s not what’s happening, and that not happening seems indeed like one of the most predictable attributes of how a racing strategy would go.

(Also, to be clear, I am using SURA here for the sake of conversational fluidity. I don’t think it carves reality at its joints as I am discussing in the other thread.)

Scott Alexander: “But you are generally much more in favor of the power-seeking strategies of people in DC than I am. Those people are mostly against SURA, though occasionally in-favor.”

This doesn’t seem to cleave reality at its joints to me. Power-seeking in this context =? trying to get the ability to get laws passed. You want laws passed. I want laws passed. In 90% of cases they’re the same laws, because our differences are mostly about what to do in situations where we can’t get good enough laws to constrain race dynamics.

I think the closest thing to a real difference that you’re noticing is that it’s easier for me to make alliances with people who want incremental change, because forcing AI companies to spend a bit more on alignment matters to me, whereas I don’t think it matters as much to you. I think these people are pushing for incremental change rather than immediate freakout partly because some of them only believe in incremental change, and partly because they think this is more likely to get them the laws they want. I think you don’t face that temptation because there isn’t much you want incrementally.

I think that “me and my coalition just need to get as much lead as possible” is explanatory mostly when discussing Chinese chip sanctions, which I think the people who support are honest about why they support it, and which I think is a natural coalition with patriots who want us to lead for normal reasons. I don’t think there’s much effort to get Anthropic a lead over OpenAI or vice versa in a regulatory capture sense, and I don’t even know which of those are vs. aren’t in my coalition (I think it’s more likely Anthropic will be, but not so overwhelmingly more that it’s a high priority of mine to kneecap OpenAI over this).

Oliver Habryka: I think I’ll throw in my hat here on this thread. I think there are large differences between the strategies we seem to be excited about in DC. I think some ways of getting the power to get laws passed is good, and others are bad.

> Chinese chip sanctions, which I think the people who support are honest about why they support it

What are you talking about. No RAND paper connected with the chip export controls has ever been honest about the author’s motivation for why they support it. None of them mention existential or catastrophic risk, or how a race towards powerful AI might be bad, at least when I last skimmed through them a few months ago.

Indeed the chip sanctions are my standard go-to example of how our friends in DC are building policy coalitions under covers that are completely disconnected from a huge fraction of their true beliefs (and they have also just told me they are doing that).

Oliver in the above exchange is trying to illustrate the contrast between speaking openly and directly about what you want to do and why you want to do it, versus machinations where you attempt to gain influence and power in and for DC in other ways and via other arguments, as an instrumentally convergent strategy. Scott doesn’t understand why Oliver and I think that contrast is important.

Yes, there was an organization that shifted from a 100% discount to a 90% discount after Scott put out a series of Twitter posts on related subjects, that they considered quite harmful and in bad faith. They also continue to work with Scott in other ways. That seems entirely reasonable to me, and I agreed with their assessment that the Twitter posts in question were quite bad and harmful. I disagree with much of the post we are now discussing, but it is much better.

There were extensive additional discussions between Oliver and Scott, such as here. Oliver gathered his highlights into this longform comment on Scott’s OP.

Why do Anthropic and OpenAI get the most criticism by far on LessWrong over other labs? Because they are the labs that matter, and that listen, and are worthy of criticism. Why would you bother criticizing Meta? Anthropic gets modestly more complaints than OpenAI for the same reasons.

There has been a shift towards more Plan A efforts versus Plan C efforts, but the vast majority of the efforts are still Plan C efforts, even if you don’t count Anthropic.

Daniel Kokotajlo: I don’t really know the people you are criticizing, I spend most of my time talking to people advocating for Plan C. You say the pendulum has swung too far, maybe it has, but not in the community around me as far as I can tell.

I think there is still too much energy going into “oh well, let’s try to make Plan C less bad, that’s the best we can do” strategies relative to how much energy is going into “Let’s try to make Plan A more likely” strategies. I agree it is possible to go too far, for the reasons you mention, but at least the part of the community around me doesn’t seem to have gone far enough yet. YMMV.

It’s Not the Incentives, It’s You

Scott Alexander asks, are corporate incentives The One Ring that inevitably corrupts? Are mass movement incentives similar?

Is it okay if, in the end, you are indeed corrupted, provided you can do enough along the way, as was famously true of the fictional OG Frodo Baggins? One could say that the lesson of Frodo Baggins is partly that you need a plan for when you get corrupted.

Daniel Kokotajlo: I think corporate incentives basically ARE the One Ring with massive corrupting influence. However, I also agree that mass movement politics can be like this too.

However, for most individuals, it’s pretty clear which corrupting influence is stronger. Ask yourself questions like the following:

  1. Am I inside an AI company’s offices right now?
  2. Have I been inside such offices in the last month?
  3. Check my bank account — where is the money coming from?
  4. List my top ten friends, and the most recent ten people I talked to. How many of them work at AI companies?
  5. OK, what about fancy think tanks that cultivate relationships with the big AI companies?
  6. OK, on the flip side: Have I been to an anti-AI protest in the last month? Have I ever?
  7. Have I ever said anything in public like “The companies should stop unilaterally? How about in the last week?
  8. Have I ever shunned anyone for working at an AI company?
  9. If I got a job at an AI company tomorrow to work on AI safety stuff, would my friends shun me?”

By asking and answering simple questions like this, I think you’ll pretty quickly be able to figure out which corrupting influence is more applicable to you. We each should try to resist the corrupting influence that applies most strongly to us.

Anthropic Is Not Optimally Pursuing These Plans

Scott’s post largely frames the decision of Anthropic or other major labs as either ‘disband your company or at least outright pause’ versus not doing so.

There are many things Anthropic is not doing but could do, that do not involve disbanding the company, fully pausing AI R&D or even doing anything terribly costly, that would greatly improve our situation.

Daniel Kokotajlo: Right now even Anthropic’s lobbyists seem to be pushing for weak sauce things instead of advocating for good ASI-pilled policies; if their whole company stopped development, perhaps that would also (like Cortez burning his ships) get them to pivot to advocate for better things.

I agree it still probably won’t work, and I don’t think it’s the best strategy they could take, but I hold it up as a sort of “control group” for strategies they could take, since I think every single one of these companies right now is currently pursuing a strategy that’s even worse than stopping unilaterally. I don’t want them to feel morally OK with what they are doing now, and I want them to know that what they are doing now is probably worse than stopping unilaterally.

TsviBT: It seems like this post argues about a dichotomy “either SURA, or race & align”. E.g. your counterfactual is “Anthropic disbanded their entire company immediately with the explicit goal of raising awareness of a pause”. But this dichotomy doesn’t make sense to me even under your assumptions, as an answer to “What should Anthropic do?”. For example, here’s a different thing that Anthropic could do:

  • Stay at the frontier in order to do frontier-level alignment research, but don’t release leading models. (If you’re going to say, well, they need to make money–do they? Is second place not making money? If second place doesn’t make much money, and really it’s just Anthropic and OpenAI neck-and-neck, doesn’t that somewhat put the lie to “Anthropic is barely making the race go faster.”?)
  • Clearly, repeatedly, strongly commit to a conditional, indefinite stop on all frontier AI R&D.
  • Support strong binding regulation on AI R&D.
  • Aggressively publicly advocate for a global stop. Fine, make it conditional. But an actual stop, advocated clearly and consistently.
  • Actively build bridges with other AI research groups.
  • Aggressively negotiate for a stop with other research groups.
  • Other stuff that one thinks of when one sincerely wants to stop and then actually tries, as opposed to insincerely.

And on a smaller scale, I for one am, I suppose, a SURA guy, but I also encourage people to stay and seriously investigate how to get a stop / why their lab can’t stop / who to organize with to get a stop / how to talk to other labs. You seem to have a lot of energy for defending that they should keep doing AI R&D, and seem to only mention

I would hope the people we’re talking about (the most alignment-pilled people at major companies) would be doing anti-AI activism, and donating some of their money to anti-AI activism, regardless of whether or not they quit. All quitting does is give them less of a platform and less money.

in the comments in order to counter the argument that it would be impactful if all these people quit and advocated for a stop. You hope that they would do that, great, me too–where’s the energy for that?

Your section “V.A: Getting companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner” seems to somewhat agree with the spirit of this. But if Anthropic are the good guys, why aren’t they doing this?

How much has Anthropic as a whole spent on getting a pause? It has $billions in spending and thousands of employees. What do we have from it, supporting a pause? A few essays, a paper or two, and other bits and bobs? Where’s the staffed team? Where’s the sustained inter-lab and international outreach? Where’s the PR campaign for a stop? Where’s the lobbying for an actual stop? This is not even a defensible effort, let alone a sincere and serious effort.

You say:

My very preliminary model would be that this halves our chance of getting that 20%pp bonus of going from Plan D -> Plan C+ (and so costs us 10%pp).

But what about the chances that Anthropic will safetywash / sanitywash pushing forward RSI? What about the chances that the main difference between them and OpenAI is that they’ll do more handwringing and have slightly better “alignment”-patching and warning-shot masking? What about if they maneuver so that they get to continue doing AI R&D, at the cost of a pause, in the name of “well maybe the pause won’t be perfect and so we’d be giving up our precious lead”?

If someone is really, truly forced to pick up into their own hands the tools to destroy the entire world, ok. But they should be terrified of this, and should seek at all times, with as much energy as they can spare, to get out of that situation!

Scott Alexander: I mostly agree with you – I don’t think my claim hinges on whether current companies are perfect or even necessarily good, it’s that part of our goal should push them towards being better (while still “in the race”).

… I’m unclear on what Anthropic’s opinion on / level of work towards a pause is. The Pacing The Frontier letter seemed like a statement that they were aiming for it.

TsviBT: The presumptive fact that there’s a grossly insufficient amount of serious effort towards a global stop coming from Anthropic, implies that so far all the hundreds or thousands of people who were conflicted about joining, and then joined, haven’t caused a non-grossly-insufficient effort. This is a strong argument against the value of joining.

Against Against Sura

For the purposes of discussing what to do next, let us break up SURA into Absurd SURA, Strong SURA and Weak SURA, and then there is non-SURA.

Absurd SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to tell countries to ban AI capabilities development, labs to shut down and employees to quit.

I call it ‘Absurd SURA’ because this is an obviously dumb strawman. Disregard.

Strong SURA says the only ethical or valid action is to stop developing AI capabilities. Ideally one would coordinate with other nations or labs to do so. But, failing that, nations must ban AI capabilities development, labs must shut down and employees must quit. It is not worth investing in a fallback plan, and indeed it is at least arguably better not to help the labs with their prosaic alignment as this prevents warning shots.

I think this is a valid position to take. It is right if one believes that prosaic alignment plans as could potentially be implemented by Anthropic or OpenAI are doomed. As in, if you think that a realistic ‘Plan C+’ very likely causes everyone to die.

Weak SURA says that you should fight hard for Plan A and for a coordinated pause, that on the margin more employees should loudly quit, and that if coordination is unsuccessful then labs and nations should soon point pause even on their own, if capabilities advance the way the labs predict they will advance. But that a better execution of Plan C can matter a lot too, so you should also simultaneously strive to maximize our chances of a good execution of Plan C.

Non-SURA is opposed even to Weak SURA, and prefers to optimize Plan C. It tries to back ‘the good guys’ which typically means America and Anthropic, and to ensure they have as big a lead as possible.

Scott Alexander spends his post arguing against at least Strong SURA.

My position on this is that I respect advocates of Strong SURA, I am walking the path of Weak SURA, and I reject both Absurd SURA and non-SURA.

Should you treat lab employees as deontologically evil people? I say no. Nor do you need to shun or be rude to them. But I do think you should treat them, whether or not they have good reason to do it, as participating in a deontologically evil thing. When you are building a thing that might kill everyone there might be no better play available, but also you should seriously consider maybe not doing that.
